mainEntity.name: Will brushing too hard immediately damage my crown margin?

acceptedAnswer.text: Damage from over-vigorous brushing is generally a gradual process rather than an immediate event. The gum tissue is resilient but can be worn down with repeated trauma over weeks, months, or years. The underlying tooth structure and cement may also be slowly affected. This is why it is important to establish good brushing technique early, particularly if you have crown restorations. If you are concerned, your dentist or hygienist can assess your current technique and gum health at your next appointment.

mainEntity.name: How do I know if my crown margin is exposed?

acceptedAnswer.text: Some patients notice a visible line or change in colour at the gumline of a crowned tooth, which may indicate that the margin is becoming exposed due to gum recession. Others experience sensitivity or discomfort in that area. However, it is not always possible to assess this at home, as the margin may be partially below the gumline. A dental examination, sometimes combined with X-rays, is the most reliable way to assess the integrity of a crown margin. Please do not attempt to probe or investigate the area yourself.

mainEntity.name: Is an electric toothbrush better for crowned teeth?

acceptedAnswer.text: Electric toothbrushes can be very effective for patients with crowns, particularly models that include a pressure indicator. These devices alert the user when too much force is being applied, which can help prevent brushing trauma around the gum margin. Oscillating-rotating and sonic electric toothbrushes have both been shown to be effective at plaque removal. The key, however, is technique — an electric toothbrush used with excessive pressure can still cause harm. Your dentist or hygienist can advise on the most appropriate toothbrush for your situation.

mainEntity.name: How long do dental crowns typically last?

acceptedAnswer.text: The lifespan of a dental crown varies depending on the material used, the location in the mouth, the patient's oral hygiene habits, and individual factors such as bite force or grinding habits. Many crowns can last ten years or more with good maintenance, and some last considerably longer. However, crowns are not considered permanent and will eventually need assessment and potentially replacement. Regular dental check-ups allow your dentist to monitor the condition of your crowns and advise on any concerns before they become significant problems.

mainEntity.name: Can gum recession around a crown be treated?

acceptedAnswer.text: Gum recession around a crowned tooth depends on the cause and severity. In early stages, improving oral hygiene habits and brushing technique may help stabilise the situation and prevent further recession. In more advanced cases, periodontal (gum) treatments may be recommended to address underlying gum disease. Severe recession that exposes a significant portion of the crown margin may require assessment for possible gum grafting procedures or crown replacement. Any treatment decisions would be made following a thorough clinical examination by a qualified dental professional.

mainEntity.name: Should I tell my dentist if I think I brush too hard?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes — absolutely. Your dentist and dental hygienist are well-placed to assess the impact of your brushing habits on your teeth and gums, and to offer practical, personalised guidance. There is no need to feel embarrassed. Many patients inadvertently brush too hard, often because they believe it leads to cleaner teeth. During a routine appointment, your hygienist can demonstrate effective brushing technique and advise on the right tools for your individual needs.
